description:
PhD Stipend & Salary Comparison by Country (2027 Rates)

Direct answer box (first 50 words):

A PhD stipend comparison only works if you compare net income, not headline numbers. In 2027 rates, UK stipends run roughly £18,700–£21,000 tax-free, German TV-L E13 positions pay €4,000+ gross (about €2,300–€2,600 net at 65–75% contracts), Dutch PhD employees earn €2,900–€3,700 gross per month, and Japanese MEXT pays ¥144,000–¥145,000 monthly.

The number that matters: net income after real costs

Advertised figures mislead in three ways: some are gross salaries with tax and social security deducted, some are tax-free stipends, and none by themselves tell you what tuition, insurance and rent will consume. Before comparing offers, convert everything to this formula:

Monthly net pay − rent − health insurance − tuition gap − commuting = real disposable income.

A "lower" stipend in a cheap city can outperform a "higher" salary in an expensive one. Our guide to building a PhD living-cost budget for the UK, Germany and the Netherlands walks through the full calculation city by city.

2027 stipend and salary rates at a glance

Sources: funding bodies' published 2026–27 rates (Gates Cambridge, Rhodes Trust, DAAD, MEXT, SERI, Dutch CLB collective agreement). Always verify the current year's rate on the official page before making decisions — and cross-check individual listings on NextApply's fully funded scholarships page.

UK: the stipend model

UK PhD funding is a scholarship stipend, not a salary. It is tax-free and National Insurance-free, which makes a £19,000 stipend worth roughly the same disposable income as a ~£23,000 taxable salary. Two catches:

  1. Fee status. The stipend usually sits on top of tuition, and international fee status can double or triple what the funder must cover. Always check whether a "fully funded" advert covers overseas fees — our guide on spotting whether a PhD is truly funded for international students shows exactly what to look for.
  2. London weighting. Some funders (including UKRI and Gates Cambridge) pay a higher London rate; others do not adjust at all.

Germany: the employment model

Most German doctoral researchers in STEM are employees. The TV-L E13 pay group at 65–75% of full time means:

  • Gross pay well above most stipends internationally, reduced by tax and social security
  • Employer-funded pension and health insurance — you do not buy separate cover
  • Paid vacation and strong worker protections

The same gross figure can look very different depending on your contract percentage and pay step. Read our TV-L E13 explainer before comparing German offers.

Netherlands: salaried doctoral employees

Dutch universities employ PhD candidates on a fixed four-year contract with a standard rising pay scale (CLB): roughly €2,901 gross in year 1 rising to €3,707 in year 4. After taxes and contributions, expect around €2,200–€2,600 net. Some positions still exist on grant-based scholarship terms with weaker rights — our Netherlands PhD employment guide explains how to tell the difference in a vacancy text.

When "small" stipends still win

  • MEXT Japan covers tuition and airfare on top of the stipend, and several universities offer subsidised housing — the cash figure understates the package.
  • Swiss Excellence scholars get CHF 2,450/month, but Swiss salaries and rents are proportionally high; treat it as comfortable only if your host city rent is manageable.
  • Fully funded scholarships like Gates Cambridge add family allowances, airfare and development funding worth thousands per year beyond the headline stipend.

How to compare two concrete offers

  1. Write down both monthly net figures (ask HR or the funder for the net calculation — they answer this routinely).
  2. Subtract rent for a realistic flat share near each campus (university housing office figures, not listings sites).
  3. Subtract health insurance where it is not employer-provided.
  4. Subtract any tuition not covered.
  5. Divide what remains by local cost-of-living index. That final number — not the advert — is your quality of life.

For the broader trade-offs beyond money (duration, supervision style, career paths), see our UK vs Germany vs Netherlands PhD comparison.

Frequently asked questions

Is a PhD stipend taxable? UK stipends are tax-free. German and Dutch contract salaries are taxable but include social benefits. US stipends are generally taxable income. The rule: salary = usually taxed, stipend = usually not, but verify locally.

Which country pays PhD students the most in 2027? On gross pay, Switzerland and the Netherlands lead; on disposable income, Germany, the Netherlands and Scandinavia typically outperform the UK because stipends there are lower. Net-of-rent results flip by city.

Can I survive on a UK PhD stipend in London? It is tight but common — London-weighted stipends (~£21,000) plus flat sharing make it workable. Non-London cities stretch the same money considerably further.

Official sources

Rates cited above come from published 2026–27 figures by Gates Cambridge Trust, the Rhodes Trust, DAAD, MEXT, SERI and the Dutch CLB agreement. Confirm current rates on each funder's official page before accepting any offer.
